# The question

More than half of the Las Peñas campus (ESPOL, Guayaquil; 3.25 ha) is being
rebuilt. The campus sits at the foot of the Cerro del Carmen and Cerro Las
Peñas, a few metres from the Guayas river, among the last fragments of Ecuadorian
dry forest inside the city — a forest type that lost 2 632 km² between 1990 and
2018 and of which only 13 % of the coastal remnant enjoys any protection.

Before the works began there was no diagnosis of what lived there. Without one,
three things follow: the construction proceeds blind to the relative ecological
value of each zone; landscape-design decisions that could favour pollinators and
birds are made on aesthetic grounds alone; and, once it is over, there is no
reference condition against which to judge whether anything was lost.

**Counting species does not answer this.** Species richness says nothing about
what those species *do* — and it is the doing that a construction project
disrupts. This study therefore measures functional diversity: the value and the
range of the traits that determine how organisms respond to environmental
filters and how they affect ecosystem processes.

# What was measured

| | |
|---|---|
| **Zones** | 1, 3, 4, 5 (Zone 2 excluded — under construction). 13 893 m², 42.7 % of the campus |
| **Flora** | Single complete census. Abundance = crown-projection cover |
| **Fauna** | Three monthly campaigns (May–July 2026): birds by 15 m fixed-radius point counts, reptiles and pollinators by timed walks |
| **Flora traits** | Growth form, height, leaf phenology, leaf form, dispersal syndrome, LDMC, SLA |
| **Fauna traits** | Body mass, trophic guild, activity stratum |
| **Recorded** | 42 plant species (all introduced ornamentals) · 9 animal species (6 native) |

The full data dictionary — units, laboratory protocol, and the five documented
deviations from the reference protocol for LDMC and SLA — is in
[`data/README.md`](../data/README.md).

# Loading the data

```{r load}
library(ggplot2); library(cluster); library(vegan)
source("R/redundancy.R")
source("R/taxonomic_diversity.R")

rd <- function(f) read.csv(file.path("data", f), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

traits_flora <- rd("traits_flora.csv")
abund_flora  <- rd("abundance_flora.csv")
meta         <- rd("species_metadata.csv")
zones        <- rd("zones.csv")

zones[zones$evaluada == "TRUE", c("Zona","area_m2","puntos_ha","superficie_cubierta_pct")]
```

Note the fourth column before going further. Sampling effort per unit area
varies **4.4-fold** between Zone 3 (2.9 points ha⁻¹) and Zone 5 (12.9 points
ha⁻¹), and effective coverage ranges from 20.5 % to 90.9 %. Every between-zone
comparison below carries that caveat.

# Building the trait space

Traits are mixed — three continuous, four categorical for flora — so the
distance is Gower's, which handles both and rescales each numeric variable by
its range. Height and SLA are `log10`-transformed first because both are
strongly right-skewed, and Gower's range rescaling is sensitive to the extremes
that skew produces.

```{r traitspace}
prep_traits <- function(df, continuous, categorical, log_cols = character(0)) {
  rownames(df) <- df$Nombre_cientifico
  df$Nombre_cientifico <- NULL
  for (cc in log_cols)    df[[cc]] <- log10(df[[cc]])
  for (ct in categorical) df[[ct]] <- as.factor(df[[ct]])
  df[, c(continuous, categorical), drop = FALSE]
}
prep_comm <- function(abund, species_ref) {
  rownames(abund) <- abund$Nombre_cientifico
  abund$Nombre_cientifico <- NULL
  m <- t(as.matrix(abund))
  m <- m[, colnames(m) %in% species_ref, drop = FALSE]
  m <- m[rowSums(m) > 0, , drop = FALSE]
  m[, colSums(m) > 0, drop = FALSE]
}

tf <- prep_traits(traits_flora,
                  continuous  = c("H_m", "LDMC", "SLA"),
                  categorical = c("forma_crecimiento","fenologia","forma_hoja","dispersion"),
                  log_cols    = c("H_m", "SLA"))
cf <- prep_comm(abund_flora, rownames(tf))
tf <- tf[colnames(cf), , drop = FALSE]

d_flora <- cluster::daisy(tf, metric = "gower")
c(min = min(d_flora), mean = mean(d_flora), max = max(d_flora))
```

Gower distances on mixed traits are generally **not Euclidean**, which produces
negative eigenvalues in the PCoA and leaves the convex hull behind FRic
ill-defined. Two corrections are standard: Cailliez adds a constant to the
distances, Lingoes to the squared distances. Lingoes distorts less; **Cailliez
is the default in this repository because it is what produced the published
tables**, and reproducing them takes precedence over improving on them. The
choice is a one-line change and should be reported as a sensitivity check, not
made silently.

# Which indices each zone can actually support

```{r feasibility}
S <- rowSums(cf > 0)
data.frame(Zone = names(S), n_species = S,
           `FRic/FEve/FDiv` = ifelse(S >= 3, "computable", "NA — convex hull needs S ≥ 3"),
           FDis = "computable", check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
```

Zone 1 holds two plant species. No amount of computation produces a convex hull
from two points in a multidimensional space, so its FRic, FEve and FDiv are
structurally undefined — not missing, not zero. Publishing this table means the
`NA`s in the results below are explained rather than merely present.

FDis, by contrast, is defined for any non-empty community and is far less
sensitive to the number of retained axes. That is why the management
recommendations lean on it.

# Results

```{r heatmaps, out.width="100%", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics(c("figures/heatmap_flora.png", "figures/heatmap_birds.png"))
```

Two patterns dominate and they belong together.

**Functional richness is low everywhere.** The species present occupy a small
volume of trait space — the compression that urban environmental filters
reliably produce, and here amplified by a flora that is 100 % introduced
ornamentals, chosen by a landscaping budget rather than assembled by a dry
forest.

**Functional divergence is high** (0.59–1.00). The most abundant species sit
away from the centre of that small volume. A community that is compact but whose
extremes carry the abundance.

A caution on the bird panel: FRic is `NA` there because Zones 3, 4 and 5 contain
*exactly the same four species*, and an unweighted volume cannot tell identical
species lists apart. Zone 1 is the exception — the only zone with *Columba
livia* and *Quiscalus mexicanus*, two large synanthropic birds that widen the
body-mass range. That the **car park** would score the campus's highest bird
functional richness is the clearest possible argument against using any single
index as a conservation criterion.

# Species diversity is not functional diversity

```{r redundancy}
red_flora <- functional_redundancy(cf, as.matrix(d_flora))
red_flora[, c("Zone","n_species","Simpson_D","RaoQ","FR_rel")]
```

Functional redundancy (Ricotta et al. 2016) is the share of species diversity
that does **not** translate into functional diversity: `FR = D − Q`, reported as
`1 − Q/D`. It is the measurement that licenses the resilience claim. A low FRic
says the community occupies little trait space; it does *not* say that different
species do the same job. That is a separate assertion and it needs its own
number.

```{r redfig, out.width="100%", echo=FALSE}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/taxonomic_vs_functional.png")
```

> **Read [`docs/verification.md`](verification.md), item V1, before quoting a
> redundancy figure.** The thesis reports 0.79–0.88; this implementation gives
> 0.21–0.57 on the same data with the same formula. The disagreement is
> systematic and almost certainly comes down to how the dissimilarity inside Q
> was scaled. It is unresolved, and it is stated here rather than hidden,
> because the "≈87 % redundancy" figure is the single number the conclusions
> lean on hardest.

# Is any of this more than a richness effect?

This is the question a committee asks first, and until now nothing in the
pipeline could answer it. FRic, FDis and Rao's Q all rise with richness by
construction, and the zones span 2 to 26 plant species. Saying "Zone 4 is
functionally richer than Zone 3" risks saying no more than "Zone 4 has more
species", which the census already told us.

`R/null_models.R` shuffles the species labels of the **trait** matrix 999 times
while holding the community matrix — and therefore richness and the abundance
distribution — fixed:

$$\text{SES} = \frac{\text{observed} - \text{mean}(\text{null})}{\text{sd}(\text{null})}$$

- **SES < 0** — co-occurring species are *more similar* than an equally rich
  random draw: functional clustering, the expected signature of urban filtering.
- **SES > 0** — *more different* than expected: overdispersion.
- **SES ≈ 0** — the zone is a random subset of the campus pool, and the
  difference between zones is a richness difference and nothing more.

```{r nullmodels, eval=FALSE}
# Requires FD. ~2-5 minutes for flora at 999 permutations.
source("R/null_models.R")
ses <- ses_functional(tf, cf, n_perm = 999, corr = "cailliez")
subset(ses, Index %in% c("FDis", "RaoQ"))
```

One limitation is worth stating plainly: the pool is the **campus** species
list, so the test asks whether a zone is a random draw from what grows on
campus. It cannot ask whether the campus itself is filtered relative to the
regional dry-forest flora — that needs a regional pool this study did not
sample.

# The *Apis mellifera* problem

*Apis mellifera* accounted for **90.1–95.7 %** of Zone 4 fauna records. Because
FDis weights distances by relative abundance, pooling it with the vertebrates
drags the community centroid onto a single functional type and depresses the
index. Analysed separately, the effect disappears — confirming it was a
methodological artefact, not a property of the community.

Two further reasons make the separation non-negotiable rather than convenient:

1. Those counts are **extrapolated**, not observed: four 2.5 m units in *Ixora
   coccinea* planters scaled by a factor of 30.4 to the 304 m the plant occupies.
2. The units were placed in the four *longest* planters, not at random. Since
   honeybees concentrate foragers on the richest patches through dance
   recruitment, the figure is an **upper bound** — an index of visitation
   intensity per unit of floral resource, not a population size.

The `sensitivity/` outputs quantify the effect directly by recomputing every
index under raw, `log(x+1)` and presence/absence weighting. A large gap between
raw and presence *is* the dominance signal.

# What follows for the remodeling

**Conserve Zone 4 and the large-crowned trees** — *Tabebuia aurea*, *Gliricidia
sepium*, *Mangifera indica*, *Ficus benjamina*. The case does not rest on the
functional indices, which for birds do not discriminate between zones. It rests
on convergent evidence: highest plant richness (26 species), highest accumulated
crown cover (101.3 %), the only canopy stratum the frugivorous birds use, five
of the six native animal species, and the campus's only *Ixora coccinea* — the
sole floral resource on which any pollinator activity was ever observed.

**Plant for the traits that are missing, not for the species that are pretty.**
The trait matrix names three concrete gaps: 86 % of species are evergreen and
every one of the six deciduous species is an introduced tree, so **no deciduous
shrub exists on campus**; 26 % are ornamental palms, all evergreen and
zoochorous — the single most redundant block in the assemblage; and only 8 of 42
species sit at the conservative end of the leaf-economics spectrum. Native dry-
forest species that fill those gaps: *Handroanthus chrysanthus* (deciduous,
wind-dispersed, a functional substitute for the introduced *Tabebuia aurea*),
*Cordia lutea* (semi-deciduous shrub, long flowering, continuous resource for
native pollinators), *Bonellia sprucei* and *Pithecellobium excelsum*.

**Diversify the floral resource** so that the pollinator community is not one
introduced species visiting one introduced shrub.

**Re-run this pipeline after the works** with the same methods, using these
results as the reference.

# Limitations

- **Three campaigns, one season.** Sampling spans the wet-to-dry transition
  only; the full seasonal turnover is not captured.
- **Effort varies 4.4-fold** between zones (see `data/zones.csv`). Rarefaction
  helps for counts; it does not fully correct this.
- **No before–after design and no unintervened control.** Future change cannot
  be attributed unambiguously to the remodeling — the reference condition
  supports description, not causal inference.
- **Small n throughout.** Four zones and 2–26 species per zone leave little room
  for inferential statistics; the null models are the appropriate tool at this
  scale, and even they need the caveat above.
- **LDMC is systematically overestimated** (no rehydration before fresh-mass
  determination) and leaf subsamples came from a single individual per species.
  Relative ordering along the leaf-economics axis holds — which is what Gower
  uses — but the absolute values are not comparable to TRY or GLOPNET.
- **Open verification items.** See [`docs/verification.md`](verification.md).
  The redundancy discrepancy (V1) is unresolved.
